questions.prompt: You want `.env` blocked for everyone who works in this repo, in a way that travels with the project. What do you set?
options: Answer "no" every time Claude Code asks to read .env
A deny rule in the project's shared settings file, committed
A deny rule in your own project-local settings file, uncommitted
Turn on accept-all mode so it never asks
questions.explanation: A committed deny rule in the shared settings file is the one that applies to everyone and travels with the project. Option A is tempting because it works for you right now, but it is a per-conversation yes/no that helps nobody else and resets. Option C is personal and uncommitted, so it does not reach the team. Option D loosens rather than blocks.

questions.prompt: Claude Code edits `src/auth/login.py` without asking, but minutes ago it asked before editing a different file. Why?
options: It is ignoring the permission system
A previous yes is in scope — you already allowed edits to that path, so it does not re-ask
It only asks once per session
Edits to auth files are always allowed
questions.explanation: Permission scope is per-tool and per-path, so a prior yes to that path is why it stays quiet now. Option A is the tempting read when prompting looks inconsistent, but the inconsistency is the scope you already granted. Option C is too broad — the tool still asks for new tools and paths. Option D invents a special case that does not exist.

questions.prompt: Earlier this session you said yes to reading `.env`. Now a deny rule for `Read(.env)` is in effect. You ask it to read `.env`. What happens?
options: The earlier yes wins — it reads the file
Deny always wins: it refuses, even though you allowed it earlier
It asks you to confirm the deny
questions.explanation: Deny beats allow — if a path is denied, no tool touches it, which is one of the few hard rules in the system. Option A is tempting because an explicit yes feels stronger than a rule, but the ordering is the other way. Option C is not how a deny works; there is nothing to confirm. Option D inverts the precedence.

questions.prompt: You open a folder Claude Code has never seen. It asks "do you trust this folder?" What is that prompt?
options: A convenience ask you can silence with accept-all
The security boundary — the one prompt that decides whether the folder is trusted at all
A per-file permission for the first file it reads
questions.explanation: The folder-trust prompt is the boundary; everything after it is fineness over an already-trusted folder. Option A is the tempting confusion the reframe targets: accept-all smooths the per-action prompts, not the boundary. Option C confuses the one prompt per folder with the many prompts per file. Option D mixes the boundary up with a sandbox over edits.
